title: Faustina Kowalska (1905–1938)
hook: a Polish sister records a message of mercy: Jesus, I trust in you

segments.voice: Yesterday, Padre Pio, the friar with the long line outside his confessional. Your line was pray, hope, don't worry. Did those words catch a worry? Today, a sister who worked in kitchens and gardens and wrote in a notebook. Day nine hundred six.

A painter's studio in Vilnius. A priest has hired an artist to paint a picture to a nun's description. She comes in to check on it. Jesus in a white robe, one hand raised in blessing, the other touching his chest, where two rays stream out, one pale and one red. The nun looks at the canvas, and, by her own account in her diary, she goes away and weeps, because it isn't as beautiful as what she saw. Her name is Sister Faustina Kowalska.
screen: `A PAINTER'S STUDIO.` → `TWO RAYS, ONE PALE, ONE RED.` → `SHE WEEPS AT THE CANVAS.`

segments.voice: Her life comes in four pieces. First, the ordinary work. She came from a poor farming family in Poland, worked as a housekeeper, then joined a congregation of sisters. There she did the plain jobs: cook, gardener, the sister at the gate. Second, the message. She wrote that Jesus spoke to her about his mercy, asked for the image to be painted, and asked that it carry a signature: Jesus, I trust in you. At her confessor's request, she wrote down what she experienced in a diary, which became a long book. Third, the chaplet. She recorded a short prayer, prayed on ordinary rosary beads, that keeps asking for mercy on us and on the whole world. It takes a few minutes. Catholics pray it at home, in hospitals, and at three in the afternoon, the hour tradition links to Jesus's death. Fourth, the old word. Divine Mercy was not a new idea. Psalm one hundred thirty-five, in the Douay-Rheims, repeats one refrain over and over: "for his mercy endureth for ever." Faustina's message sends people back to that refrain, with a name and a face attached, and asks for one thing in return: trust. Not trust that life will go smoothly. Faustina was ill for years and died young. Trust, as she wrote of it, that mercy is bigger than anything a person has done. The Church later canonized her, and her image now hangs in churches far from Poland, the rays still pale and red, the line still underneath.
screen: `A COOK AND A GARDENER.` · `A NOTEBOOK OF MERCY.` · `A CHAPLET ON ROSARY BEADS.` · `AN OLD REFRAIN.` · then, large: `HIS MERCY ENDURETH FOR EVER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray the chaplet once. The whole chaplet takes longer than this sit, so begin it now and finish after, or simply start. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, take rosary beads or use your fingers, and on each bead ask for mercy on yourself and on the whole world, in the chaplet's words or your own. If you don't pray, let one face come to mind, someone you find hard to forgive, and hold it for a moment without judging it. Then rest. The bell holds the time.
Divine Mercy. God's mercy, as Saint Faustina's diary and image present it, summed up in five words: Jesus, I trust in you.
Your line: jesus, I trust in you. Today, look for the image if a church near you has it, or find it online, and read the line at the bottom. Day nine hundred six.

howItsDone: Catholics who keep this devotion pray the Divine Mercy chaplet on rosary beads, often at three in the afternoon, and the image with its signature 'Jesus, I trust in you' hangs in parish churches; the Sunday after Easter is kept as Divine Mercy Sunday.

fork.setup: you're Faustina. you've described an image, and a painter has finished it. it's not as beautiful as what you saw. what do you do?
fork.reveal: by her own account she wept. the image was kept, and it still carries the line: Jesus, I trust in you.

notes: Year-two day 666 (Divine Mercy Sunday) covered the feast, John 20 and the restriction and lifting of the devotion; this day takes her life, the image and the chaplet instead.
Painting in Vilnius by Eugeniusz Kazimirowski at Fr. Michael Sopoćko's request, and her weeping over it: from the Diary; confirm.
Image details (white robe, hand raised, two rays, pale and red): confirm.
'Churches far from Poland' and howItsDone 'parish churches' are general; Keeper may soften under the claims rule.
